Polyfill Promise.any

Promise.any is the mirror image of Promise.all: it resolves with the first fulfilled value and rejects only if every promise rejects, with an AggregateError holding all reasons in input order. Compare: race settles with the first to settle (fulfilled or rejected), and allSettled never rejects. Use case: query several mirrors and take whichever answers first.
Implement a minimal Promise (then chaining, catch, async resolution)

The essentials: three states and a value; settle only once; store callbacks while pending; then returns a new promise resolved with the callback's return value (or rejected if it throws); callbacks always run asynchronously as microtasks; and a returned promise is adopted, which is what makes chaining flatten. The full Promises/A+ spec adds a few more edge cases (such as rejecting when a promise resolves to itself).
setInterval using setTimeout, with a way to stop it

Recursive setTimeout guarantees a gap of delay between the end of one run and the start of the next, while setInterval fires on a fixed schedule and can pile up calls if the callback (or an async request it starts) takes longer than the interval. That's why polling code often uses this pattern. Timers are minimum delays, not exact: they wait for the call stack and earlier tasks.
Render a template string: "Hello {{name}}, you have {{count}} messages"

String.prototype.replace with a global regex and a callback is the key tool: the callback receives the whole match and each capture group. If the output goes into HTML, escape the values (&, <, >, quotes) to prevent XSS; frameworks like Angular do this for you in interpolation. O(n) in the template length.
Convert between camelCase, snake_case, kebab-case and Title Case

Normalise every format into a list of lower-case words first, then join them in the target style; this keeps each converter to one line. A common real use is mapping snake_case JSON from a backend (for example PHP or Python) to camelCase objects in the front end.
Shuffle an array fairly (Fisher–Yates) and pick a random element

Fisher–Yates gives every permutation an equal chance in O(n) time. The popular sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5) trick is biased, because sorting algorithms assume a consistent comparator, and it costs O(n log n). For anything security-related (tokens, OTPs) use crypto.getRandomValues or crypto.randomUUID() instead of Math.random.
Spread vs Object.assign vs structuredClone vs JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())

| {...obj} / Object.assign | structuredClone | JSON round trip
Depth | Shallow (nested objects shared) | Deep | Deep
Date, Map, Set | Shared references | Copied correctly | Date → string, Map/Set → {}
undefined, NaN | Kept | Kept | undefined properties dropped, NaN → null
Circular references | Fine (shared) | Supported | Throws TypeError
Functions, class instances | Copied by reference / own props only | Functions throw; instances become plain objects | Functions dropped; instances become plain objects
Rule of thumb: spread for one-level updates (React/NgRx state), structuredClone for a true deep copy of data, the JSON trick only for plain JSON-shaped data.
Map vs plain object as a dictionary

| Map | Object
Key types | Anything (objects, numbers, NaN) | Strings and symbols (numbers become strings)
Order | Insertion order | Integer-like keys ascending first, then strings in insertion order
Size | map.size | Object.keys(o).length
Inherited keys | None | Prototype keys like toString unless Object.create(null)
Iterate | for (const [k, v] of map) | Object.entries(o)
JSON | Needs Object.fromEntries(map) | Native
Rule of thumb: Map for counters, caches (LRU) and keys that come from user input or are not strings; object for fixed-shape records and anything sent as JSON.
for...in vs for...of vs forEach

| for...in | for...of | arr.forEach
Gives you | Keys (as strings) | Values | Value, index, array
Works on | Any object, including inherited enumerable keys | Iterables: arrays, strings, Map, Set | Arrays (and NodeList, Map, Set have their own)
break / continue | Yes | Yes | No (return only skips one item)
await inside | Works | Works, runs one by one | Does not wait: callbacks start together
On arrays | Avoid: string indexes, extra props | Best choice | Fine for simple side effects
Rule of thumb: for...of for arrays and anything async, Object.entries + for...of for objects, forEach only for short synchronous side effects.
Mutating vs non-mutating array methods (sort vs toSorted)

| Mutates the array | Returns a new array
Sort | sort() (also returns the same array) | toSorted() (ES2023)
Reverse | reverse() | toReversed()
Insert / remove | splice(), push, pop, shift, unshift | toSpliced(), slice(), concat(), spread
Replace one item | arr[i] = x, fill() | with(i, x)
Transform | n/a | map, filter, flat
Interview tip: const sorted = arr.sort() also changes arr, a classic bug with Angular inputs and signal state. Use toSorted() or [...arr].sort(), and remember the default sort compares strings, so pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.
